target.title: feat: add readiness conditions and providers
target.body:
Related RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/33

## Problem

OpenClaw already exposes Gateway `/ready` and `/readyz`, but readiness is evaluated by a fixed set of Gateway checks. Hosts and operators cannot select the additional criteria that define readiness for a deployment, plugins cannot contribute bounded observational evidence, and CLI, health, and status surfaces do not share one canonical result.

That leaves Docker, Kubernetes, systemd, OCC, and other hosts maintaining private scripts to answer a basic question: is this OpenClaw instance ready to accept work under its configured requirements?

## Proposal

This draft implements the readiness portion of RFC 0018:

- normalize Gateway startup, admission, drain, selected-channel, suppressed-channel, event-loop, configuration, plugin, and workspace evidence into structured conditions
- distinguish required conditions, which fail readiness on `False` or `Unknown`, from advisory conditions, which remain visible without changing the ready result
- let operators select built-in and plugin-contributed criteria directly with `gateway.readiness`
- let activated plugins register namespaced, self-describing criteria through the public plugin registry
- bound plugin checks with per-criterion timeouts, an overall readiness deadline, stable redacted timeout/error results, short caching, and in-flight coalescing that never duplicates a callback still pending after timeout
- return a required `ReadinessEvaluationComplete=Unknown` condition if canonical evaluation times out or fails, rather than hanging or rejecting health/status requests
- project the same canonical result through `/ready`, `/readyz`, Gateway `ready`, health, status, and `openclaw ready`
- provide human-readable and `--json` CLI output with fail-closed exit status

Example operator selection:

```json5
{
  gateway: {
    readiness: {
      requiredCriteria: ["openclaw.workspace-writable", "plugin.example.dependency"],
      advisoryCriteria: ["plugin.metrics.exporter"],
    },
  },
}
```

Core selector IDs are configuration identities: selecting `openclaw.workspace-writable` emits the stable canonical `WorkspaceWritable` condition. Plugin criteria use their full namespaced ID as the condition type.

A plugin may contribute observational evidence without changing readiness by default:

```ts
api.registerReadinessCriterion({
  id: "dependency",
  description: "Example dependency is reachable",
  async check({ pluginConfig, signal }) {
    const reachable = await probeDependency(pluginConfig, { signal });
    return reachable
      ? { status: "True", reason: "DependencyReachable", message: "Dependency is reachable." }
      : { status: "False", reason: "DependencyUnavailable", message: "Dependency is unavailable." };
  },
});
```

Core publishes that registration as `plugin.<plugin-id>.dependency`. Operators explicitly select it in `requiredCriteria` when it belongs in their serving contract.

## Compatibility

Existing `/ready` and `/readyz` routes retain their HTTP contract: `200` when all required conditions are true and `503` otherwise. Existing installations need no readiness configuration. The universal Gateway lifecycle baseline always applies; explicitly selected criteria add deployment-specific evidence.

This PR does **not** add hosting profiles, profile selection, node-mode profiles, runtime activation identity, release conformance, Lobster concepts, tenant concepts, OCC resources, or policy/Doctor dependencies. Standard Hosting Profiles are separated into RFC 0023 so this readiness facility can stand on its own.

## Review Stack

This is one upstream PR with four commits. The fork PRs preserve the same smaller review boundaries:

- [PR 17: canonical Gateway readiness conditions](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/17)
- [PR 22: workspace writability criterion](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/22)
- [PR 23: selectable readiness providers](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/23)
- [PR 27: canonical `openclaw ready` CLI](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/27)

The implementation is rebased onto OpenClaw main `4e78d91c0f96`.

## Validation

- exact head: `17b34f792d87da05ff1b4d1e99587f96f08e0dde`
- all 19 changed test files pass across eight selected Vitest project shards and 211 assertions
- Oxfmt passes on 59 changed TypeScript/JavaScript/Markdown files; Oxlint passes on 54 changed TypeScript/JavaScript files; `git diff --check` passes
- plugin SDK surface validation passes at the exact post-harvest budget: 328 public entrypoints and 10,615 public exports, with no forbidden package subpaths
- package build, public SDK declaration graph, package inventory, and tarball integrity checks pass
- ClawSweeper found the pre-rebase patch correct; this exact-head rebase removes the requested changelog entry and passes the source, SDK, and build gates below
- package-installed Docker proof on patch-equivalent head `89d8607aab9f` passes with image `sha256:8add3c4f8ce2f1a444a735c43f19eac4ee0212778123fb883ff8f9f785a9fd0d`
- `/ready` and `/readyz` transition `200 -> 503 -> 200` when a required workspace is removed and restored; `/healthz` remains `200`; `openclaw ready --json` exits `0 -> 1 -> 0` with the same `WorkspaceWritable / WorkspaceMissing` condition

`pnpm check:changed` is not claimed locally: this linked WSL worktree delegates that command to Blacksmith Testbox, and the local credential cannot access the `openclaw` organization. The changed-file tests and local static/package gates above passed; GitHub CI remains authoritative for repository-wide lanes.

## Published Upgrade Proof

The repository's `published-upgrade-survivor` Docker lane passed from the current published `openclaw@2026.7.1` package to a `2026.7.2` tarball carrying this four-commit readiness patch.

```text
OPENCLAW_UPGRADE_SURVIVOR_PUBLISHED_BASELINE=1 \
OPENCLAW_UPGRADE_SURVIVOR_BASELINE_SPEC=openclaw@2026.7.1 \
OPENCLAW_UPGRADE_SURVIVOR_CANDIDATE=current \
NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=16384 \
  bash scripts/e2e/upgrade-survivor-docker.sh
```

The lane installed and configured 2026.7.1 first, seeded agents, sessions, workspaces, credentials, channel/plugin settings, and legacy plugin dependency state, validated the baseline, upgraded the same installation through `openclaw update`, ran non-interactive Doctor and config validation, and revalidated preserved state before starting the candidate Gateway.

All 54 recorded phases passed on proved head `e5f5e97332e5495e65c1993dba258109849bdece`. Gateway startup took 47 seconds, `/healthz` 1 second, `/readyz` 1 second, and RPC status 2 seconds. The current head is rebased onto `4e78d91c0f96`. It preserves the four readiness commits, removes the release-owned changelog line requested by review, adapts the shared Gateway request-context type to current main, and refreshes the intentional Plugin SDK budgets and API baseline. Exact-head changed tests, formatting, lint, SDK checks, and the full package build pass; the package-installed Docker and published-upgrade results above remain the immediately preceding runtime compatibility evidence.

Compatibility is explicit: the upgraded existing installation did not silently acquire `WorkspaceWritable` or another opt-in criterion as a new requirement. Its existing Gateway lifecycle baseline remained ready. An operator who explicitly requires workspace writability receives the intended fail-closed transition and matching CLI exit status.

target.title: fix(agents,cron): remove pattern field from model-facing cron tool schema
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/107449

The model-facing cron tool JSON Schema includes `pattern: "\\S"` on the `declarationKey` field. llama.cpp rejects unanchored regex patterns in JSON Schemas — its grammar parser (`json-schema-to-grammar.cpp:348-352`) requires patterns to start with `^` and end with `$`. This breaks cron tool availability for any agent running through a llama.cpp backend.

## User Impact

- llama.cpp users can now use cron tools without schema parse errors
- `minLength: 1` still guarantees the field is non-empty (same effect as `pattern: "\\S"`)
- Gateway-side whitespace guard (`declarationKey.trim().length === 0`) is unchanged — stricter validation at the gateway layer
- Net change: 1 line removed in 1 file

## Evidence

### Proof 1: llama.cpp runtime validation — BEFORE vs AFTER

This uses the **exact same `nlohmann::ordered_json` library and the exact same validation logic** as llama.cpp's `json-schema-to-grammar.cpp:348-352`:

```cpp
// llama.cpp common/json-schema-to-grammar.cpp:348-352 (verbatim)
std::string _visit_pattern(const std::string & pattern, const std::string & name) {
    if (!(pattern.front() == '^' && pattern.back() == '$')) {
        _errors.push_back("Pattern must start with '^' and end with '$'");
        return "";
    }
    // ...
}
```

Compiling and running against the actual nlohmann JSON library used by llama.cpp:

```
$ g++ -std=c++17 -I llama-src/vendor -o grammar-test grammar-test.cpp && ./grammar-test
============================================================
llama.cpp JSON Schema Regex Validation — Real Source Logic
Source: json-schema-to-grammar.cpp:348-352 (_visit_pattern)
============================================================

[BEFORE FIX: pattern: \\S (unanchored)]
  pattern: "\S"
  VALIDATION: Pattern must start with '^' and end with '$'
  llama.cpp RESPONSE: HTTP 400 Bad Request
  BEFORE FIX: pattern: \\S (unanchored) → REJECTED ✓

[AFTER FIX:  no pattern field]
  pattern: (none)
  llama.cpp RESPONSE: 200 OK (grammar generated)
  AFTER FIX:  no pattern field → ACCEPTED ✓

============================================================
CONCLUSION
============================================================
  BEFORE: llama.cpp REJECTS → cron tool unavailable
  AFTER:  llama.cpp ACCEPTS → cron tool works
  minLength: 1 preserves non-empty guarantee
  Gateway side .trim() guard unchanged (cron-tool.ts:1037)
```

### Proof 2: Schema comparison — BEFORE vs AFTER (TypeBox runtime)

```
$ node --version
v22.22.3

$ node --import tsx _proof-cron.ts
[BEFORE] TypeBox schema serialization:
  minLength: 1
  maxLength: 200
  pattern: \S
  → JSON Schema: { "type": "string", "minLength": 1, "maxLength": 200, "pattern": "\\S" }
  → llama.cpp REJECTS: unanchored regex

[AFTER] TypeBox schema serialization:
  minLength: 1
  maxLength: 200
  pattern: undefined (removed)
  → JSON Schema: { "type": "string", "minLength": 1, "maxLength": 200 }
  → llama.cpp ACCEPTS: no unanchored regex
```

### Proof 3: Gateway-level guard preserved (unchanged)

Source: `src/agents/tools/cron-tool.ts:1037-1041`:
```typescript
if (typeof canonicalJob.declarationKey === "string" &&
    canonicalJob.declarationKey.trim().length === 0) {
  throw new Error("declarationKey must be a non-empty string");
}
```

Test coverage: `cron-tool.test.ts:879-887` — `declarationKey: "   "` → rejects.

### Evidence Summary

| Scenario | llama.cpp Behavior |
|---|---|
| `pattern: "\S"` (unanchored) | HTTP 400 — REJECTED |
| no pattern (minLength: 1 only) | 200 OK — ACCEPTED |
| `pattern: "^\\S+$"` (anchored) | 200 OK — ACCEPTED |

## Tests

```
$ node scripts/test-projects.mjs src/agents/tools/cron-tool.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  64 passed (64)
```

All 64 tests pass. The existing test at cron-tool.test.ts:879-887 confirms gateway whitespace guard is preserved.

## Code Changes

1. **Removed `pattern: "\\S"`** from `declarationKey` in `createCronJobObjectSchema()` — llama.cpp cannot parse unanchored regex patterns
2. **`minLength: 1` stays** — guarantees non-empty string at schema level
3. **Gateway whitespace guard unchanged** (`cron-tool.ts:1037-1041`) — `declarationKey.trim().length === 0` check catches whitespace-only keys at the gateway layer

## Context capsule

This is PR1/5 in the durable-core stack. It is docs/RFC only: it proposes a narrow residual-gap durable-core boundary and proof plan for reviewer discussion before any implementation PR claims runtime behavior.

This PR does not publish a release architecture contract. It does not claim shipped runtime behavior, wake replay, CLI/Gateway controls, session handoff, external transport delivery, schema migration, or product retry/resume policy.

## Scope updated 2026-07-15

- Reframes the architecture page as **Durable Core Residual-Gap Architecture Proposal**.
- Reframes the proof page as **Durable Core Residual-Gap Compatibility Check Plan**.
- Renames the durable proposal doc slugs from retired prerelease names to proposal slugs:

### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

openai/gpt-5.3-codex-spark emitted structured OpenClaw tool calls with empty argument objects for tools that require arguments, causing schema validation to reject every call before execution.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure an isolated OpenClaw subagent with:

  • Model: openai/gpt-5.3-codex-spark
  • Runtime: agentRuntime.id: "openclaw"
  • Tools: profile: "full", with filesystem and runtime tool groups allowed.
2. Give the agent a bounded read-only task requiring file inspection and command execution.

3. Observe its tool calls and validation results.

### Expected behavior

When invoking a tool, the model should provide fields required by the exposed tool schema. For example, read requires path, exec requires command, and browser requires action.

### Actual behavior

The model emitted calls with empty arguments:

```
read({})
exec({})
browser({})
```

OpenClaw rejected them before execution:

```
Validation failed for tool "read":
  - path: must have required properties path

Received arguments:
{}
```

session_list({}) succeeded in the same run, consistent with that tool requiring no arguments.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1

### Operating system

Linux 6.17.0-1018-oracle arm64

### Install method

docker

### Model

openai/gpt-5.3-codex-spark

### Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw embedded runtime (agentRuntime.id: "openclaw") → OpenAI ChatGPT Responses transport → gpt-5.3-codex-spark

### Additional provider/model setup details

• Thinking: medium
• Transport: auto
• Fast mode: disabled
• Reproduced in two separate isolated Spark subagent runs.
• The issue occurred before the affected agent was later changed to Luna.

### Logs

```shell
text

Validation failed for tool "read":
  - path: must have required properties path

Received arguments:
{}

Validation failed for tool "exec":
  - command: must have required properties command

Received arguments:
{}

Validation failed for tool "browser":
  - action: must have required properties action

Received arguments:
{}
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

Affected: two isolated Spark subagent runs in one OpenClaw deployment.

Consequence: required-argument tools fail before execution.


### Additional information

This differs from the Kimi plain-text/XML tool-call issue in #40069. Here, OpenClaw receives structured tool calls, but Spark supplies {} instead of required arguments.

target.title: fix(browser): keep CDP cursor text previews UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where browser cursor-interactive element text could keep a lone UTF-16 high surrogate when the page preview was cut on an emoji boundary at the final 100-unit budget: unsafe `.slice` puts that lone surrogate on the CDP `returnByValue` wire, and Node `truncateUtf16Safe(..., 100)` is a no-op when the string is already length 100, so the malformed unit survives into cursor/ARIA preview text. Competing fixes that call Node/SDK `truncateUtf16Safe` inside `Runtime.evaluate` throw `ReferenceError` and empty the cursor map.

## Why This Change Was Made

Own the cut in a **page-local** surrogate-safe helper (`truncateCdpPageTextPreview`) injected via `Function#toString`, and unify the page/Node preview budget at **100**. The old page `.slice(0, 101)` / Node `100` split only papered over unsafe page slicing by forcing a second cut; once the page budget matches the final cap, Node can no longer repair a lone surrogate already present at `length === max`. Non-goals: no product/catalog changes; no live Chrome protocol redesign.

Best-fix note: do not inject `truncateUtf16Safe.toString()` alone — it closes over `sliceUtf16Safe` / surrogate helpers in `normalization-core`, so page scope would throw the same way as [#108092](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/108092).

Collision check: searched open/closed PRs for CDP cursor text truncate / `slice(0, 101)` / `truncateCdpPageTextPreview`. Related open work: [#108092](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/108092) (calls Node helper inside page evaluate — fails closed). This PR keeps a dependency-free injectable helper instead.

## User Impact

- **Before:** At the final 100-unit preview budget, an emoji straddling the cut can leave a lone high surrogate on the CDP evaluate payload; Node re-truncate at the same budget does not remove it. Approaches that reference Node `truncateUtf16Safe` in page JS fail the whole cursor-interactive collection.
- **After:** Page preview truncate is UTF-16 safe before `returnByValue`; Node still re-applies the same 100-unit cap as defense for odd evaluate payloads. Snapshot collection does not depend on Node symbols in the page.

## Evidence

Exact head: `b4834343a4cc1369ef6438b61a8ac3446b757a74`

### current-`main` / unsafe-slice negative (same fixture)

Unsafe page cut at the final budget + Node re-truncate still leaves a lone surrogate:

```bash
node --input-type=module -e 'const text="a".repeat(99)+"😀b"; const sliced=text.slice(0,100); const hasLone=s=>/[\uD800-\uDBFF](?![\uDC00-\uDFFF])/.test(s); function truncateUtf16Safe(input,maxLen){const limit=Math.max(0,Math.floor(maxLen)); if(input.length<=limit) return input; let end=limit; if(end>0&&end<input.length){const u=input.charCodeAt(end-1); if(u>=0xd800&&u<=0xdbff){const n=input.charCodeAt(end); if(n>=0xdc00&&n<=0xdfff) end-=1;}} return input.slice(0,end);} const wire=JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({text:sliced})); console.log(JSON.stringify({unsafe_slice_len:wire.text.length,wire_lone_surrogate:hasLone(wire.text),node_truncate_still_lone:hasLone(truncateUtf16Safe(wire.text,100))},null,2));'
```

```json
{
  "unsafe_slice_len": 100,
  "wire_lone_surrogate": true,
  "node_truncate_still_lone": true
}
```

Note: current `main` still uses page `.slice(0, 101)` so Node's second cut often masks the emoji-at-101 case; that asymmetry is what this PR removes by owning a UTF-16-safe cut at the real final budget (100). The negative above is the hole that appears once page and Node share that budget without a page-safe helper (and the hole `#108092`-style Node-in-page calls cannot fix).

### after fix (focused)

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp-page-text-preview.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp.test.ts
```

```text
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  47 passed (47)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 6.18s
```

Coverage includes:
- page preview keeps emoji intact at the 100-unit boundary
- unsafe `.slice` at the final budget leaves a lone surrogate that Node `truncateUtf16Safe` cannot repair; page helper keeps preview clean
- injectable expression embeds `Function#toString` helper source and does not call Node/SDK `truncateUtf16Safe`
- page-scope stand-in documents missing Node truncate symbol → `ReferenceError` (why `#108092` fails closed)

## Verification

- Exact head: `b4834343a4cc1369ef6438b61a8ac3446b757a74`
- `oxfmt` on touched files — passed
- `git diff --check` — clean
- Focused tests: 47 passed
- Mutation: temporarily restore page `.slice(0, 100)` path in the wire fixture → `node_truncate_still_lone: true`; page helper path → clean

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** page-side CDP preview truncate is UTF-16 safe at the final 100-unit budget; Node re-cap remains defense-in-depth; page expression stays free of Node/SDK helper calls.
- **Environment:** local Linux WSL2 worktree; Vitest extension-browser lane; page-scope / helper-source stand-ins without Function/eval (no Chrome required for this unit).
- **Exact commands:** (same as Evidence)
- **Observed output after fix:** 47/47 focused tests green on head `b4834343a4cc1369ef6438b61a8ac3446b757a74`
- **What was not tested:** live Chrome CDP against a real page with emoji-labeled pointer targets; full `snapshotAria` WebSocket round-trip for this specific text.

## Risk / Compatibility

**Low.** Same final preview cap (100). Removes the page-only 101 overshoot that existed to let Node repair unsafe slices. Mitigation: page-injection + JSON-wire + `#108092` ReferenceError regressions.

## Review

- Manually reviewed and verified
- AI-assisted: Yes

target.title: fix(codex): keep omitted-final source replies from releasing the turn
target.body:
Closes #106961

## What Problem This Solves

In `message_tool_only` delivery mode, the Codex app-server treated any delivered `message` source reply as terminal unless the model explicitly passed `final: false`. An agent that sent an early progress update ("on it, will report back") had its turn released immediately: the remaining tool calls and the real final reply never ran. From the user's side the agent posts one status line and then goes silent (log signal: `codex app-server turn released after terminal dynamic tool result`).

## Why This Change Was Made

The projected `final` schema control tells the model to "set true **only when** this message is intended to complete the reply" - so models naturally omit `final` on progress sends, and the runtime contradicted its own schema by terminating anyway.

This change makes inferred source-reply delivery release the turn only on explicit `final: true`, matching the generic embedded-runner contract established in #92343: intermediate delivery continues the turn, and termination follows the normal Codex `turn/completed` lifecycle.

Safety properties preserved:

- The `sourceReplyFinal` completed marker for omitted `final` is unchanged, so stranded-reply recovery still cannot re-deliver a duplicate of a delivered reply.
- Duplicate end-block suppression via `didDeliverSourceReplyViaMessageTool` is unchanged.
- Tool-owned `terminate` results and yield results still release as before.
- Mixed dynamic-tool batch semantics (`resolveTerminalDynamicToolBatchAction`) are untouched.

The `final` schema description now also tells models that omitting it keeps the turn alive, so the control is learnable instead of discipline-based.

## User Impact

Codex-backed agents on Discord/Telegram/etc. can post intermediate progress messages and keep executing until the work is done. Explicit `final: true` still stops the turn after confirmed delivery.

## Evidence

- `extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.test.ts`: 99/99 pass. Omitted-final delivered replies are now non-terminal with a completed marker; explicit `final: true` still releases across implicit sends, explicit source routes, receipt-confirmed replies, and middleware-redacted receipts.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Google Meet attendance late/early annotation would never mark a participant as `late` or `earlyLeave` when an overflow-class grace value such as `1e308` was passed. `lateAfterMinutes * 60_000` became `Infinity`, so the comparison was always false.

## Why This Change Was Made

Bound grace minutes by numeric safety (`floor(MAX_SAFE_INTEGER / 60_000)`) across CLI parsing, tool params, and runtime decoration, instead of inventing a one-day product policy. Finite windows above one day stay accepted; overflow-class values are rejected at CLI/tool boundaries and fall back to the default (5) in decoration. Tool schemas declare the matching `maximum`. Helpers live in `attendance-grace.ts` so oversized `meet.ts` / `cli.ts` / `index.ts` do not grow.

## User Impact

**Before:** Overflow-class grace input silently disabled late/early detection. Finite values above one day were accepted.

**After:** CLI/tool reject unsafe grace flags before Meet API work. Decoration falls back to 5 for overflow-class runtime values so late/early checks stay finite. Finite integers such as 1441 / 100000 remain accepted. Default 5 is unchanged.

target.title: media: agent-scoped roots expose sibling sandbox files
target.body:
## Summary
Agent-scoped media root lists include the shared `<stateDir>/sandboxes` parent. A media request from one agent can therefore pass local-path authorization for a derivable file inside another agent or session's sandbox workspace.

## Environment
- Commit: abfdfd65b850d63d75f80ac81f277272614b4745 (origin/main at time of filing)
- Surface: agent image, PDF, media-understanding, Control UI preview, and outbound attachment paths that use agent-scoped local media roots

## Steps to reproduce
1. Create a state directory with a file at `<stateDir>/sandboxes/agent-worker/secret.png`.
2. Build the standard local media roots for that state directory.
3. From an agent-scoped media path, pass those explicit roots to `assertLocalMediaAllowed` for the sibling sandbox file.
4. Read the file after authorization succeeds.

## Expected
Agent-scoped media authorization should include only the active agent or session's sandbox workspace. A path inside a sibling sandbox should fail with `path-not-allowed`.

## Actual
The shared sandboxes parent is in every default and agent-scoped roots list. The sibling path passes containment validation and its contents are readable.

## Root cause (if known)
`src/media/local-roots.ts:40` adds the whole sandboxes parent to the baseline allowlist:

```ts
return Array.from(
  new Set([
    preferredTmpDir,
    path.join(resolvedConfigDir, "media"),
    path.join(resolvedStateDir, "media"),
    path.join(resolvedStateDir, "canvas"),
    path.join(resolvedStateDir, "workspace"),
    path.join(resolvedStateDir, "sandboxes"),
  ]),
);
```

`getAgentScopedMediaLocalRoots` starts with that same broad list and only appends the active agent workspace. It never narrows the sandbox entry. `src/media/local-media-access.ts:99` has a sibling exclusion only for `workspace-*` paths and only when `localRoots` is undefined. Agent-facing call sites normally pass an explicit roots array, so that branch does not constrain the shared `sandboxes` root.

## Sibling surfaces
PR #17136 explicitly replaced broad cross-agent workspace exposure with agent-scoped workspace roots, but retained the shared sandboxes parent in the baseline list. PR #25987 separately identified the same class of host-media exposure under `<stateDir>/agents` and proposed removing that broad root; it did not cover `<stateDir>/sandboxes`. Existing sandbox media issues and fixes address making the active sandbox readable, not preventing sibling sandbox reads.

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: Explicit agent-scoped media roots authorize a file located in a sibling sandbox workspace.
Real environment tested: Production `buildMediaLocalRoots` and `assertLocalMediaAllowed` filesystem path at commit abfdfd65b850d63d75f80ac81f277272614b4745 on Windows.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: Created two sandbox scopes under an isolated temporary state directory, built the production roots, authorized the sibling path, and read its contents with the repository runner.
Evidence after fix:
```
# OBSERVED (buggy, origin/main abfdfd65b850d63d75f80ac81f277272614b4745)
AUDIT_MEDIA {"sandboxRoot":"C:\\Users\\19802\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\openclaw-media-audit-fTXovg\\sandboxes","requestedPath":"C:\\Users\\19802\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\openclaw-media-audit-fTXovg\\sandboxes\\agent-worker\\secret.png","allowed":true,"contents":"worker-only"}

# EXPECTED (correct behavior on identical input)
allowed=false
error.code="path-not-allowed"
contents=<not read>
```
Observed result after fix: Current main authorizes and reads a sibling sandbox file because the common sandboxes parent is treated as an allowed local media root.
What was not tested: No external channel upload was performed. The reproduction drove the production root builder, real filesystem containment and canonicalization, and production local media authorization directly.

target.title: fix(agents): prevent recursive task execution during model fallback
target.body:
## Problem

When a session's primary model becomes unavailable mid-session and a fallback model serves a turn that was triggered by an internal completion announcement, the fallback can misread the announced report as a directive and spawn duplicate work. In the originating incident (#92271) a fallback turn converted "background task completed" reports into new `sessions_spawn` tasks at depth 1 — re-finalizing an already-finished PR and pushing junk commits onto its branch. `maxSpawnDepth` does not catch this: the recursion is semantic (re-executing reported results), not structural.

## Invariant

> A fallback turn replying to completion announcements must not re-execute or re-spawn work already reported as completed.

Defined once at the shared fallback/run boundary, then enforced per surface — per the review feedback.

## Changes

1. **Completion announcements are marked as evidence (all harnesses).** `buildAnnounceReplyInstruction` (`src/agents/subagent-announce.ts`) now states in every variant that the announcement reports already-completed work and must not be re-executed or re-delegated, and the previous open-ended "continue the task" wording is narrowed to the original task's own remaining steps (applied to **both** parent-facing variants as of `32f17e60`; the first push had only narrowed the no-completion-message variant). This travels in message content, so embedded, CLI, and MCP-exposed harnesses all receive it.
2. **Fallback turns are identified mechanically.** `runWithModelFallback` / `runWithImageModelFallback` set `isFallback` on non-primary candidates (`ModelFallbackRunOptions`); the bit flows through the embedded run params into tool construction. Primary attempts keep their exact previous call shape.
3. **Work-spawning is blocked at the tool choke point.** `sessions_spawn` returns `forbidden` (with an instructive error) when the current run is a fallback candidate AND the turn was triggered by an internal completion announcement. The gate sits before the runtime branch, so it covers both the `subagent` and `acp` runtimes with one check.
4. **Completion-announce detection is a shared predicate.** `isCompletionAnnounceInputProvenance` (`src/sessions/input-provenance.ts`) covers `subagent_announce` plus the agent-mediated completion sources (`agent_harness_task`, media generators) and deliberately excludes `subagent_interrupted_resume`, where resuming the work is the task itself.

## Coverage matrix (per review)

| Surface | Status |
|---|---|
| Embedded runtime (`sessions_spawn`, subagent + ACP runtimes) | Mechanically enforced, unit-tested |
| CLI / MCP harnesses | Covered by the content-level evidence guard in the announcement itself |
| Cron isolated-agent embedded runs | Mechanically enforced — `isFallback` is threaded through the cron run executor alongside `allowTransientCooldownProbe` (`32f17e60`). |
| `sessions_send` / `cron` scheduling on fallback+announce turns | **Not** mechanically gated — a fallback turn replying to an announcement can still re-delegate work via inter-session messages (`sessions_send` → `queueEmbeddedAgentMessage…`) or scheduled `agentTurn` jobs. Covered only by the content-level evidence guard. Tracked as a follow-up. |
| CLI / gateway loopback `sessions_spawn` | **Not** mechanically gated by this PR — the gateway tool-resolution path constructs `sessions_spawn` above the layer where fallback is decided, so the guard inputs are not threaded there yet. Covered only by the content-level evidence guard. Tracked as a follow-up. |
| Codex-native `spawn_agent` | Owned by the `codex-rs` tool registry (`multi_agents_spec.rs`); not exposed through this repo's spawn path, so it can't be gated from here. Scoped to a `codex-rs` follow-up. |

## Tests

- `sessions-spawn-tool.test.ts`: the gate forbids fallback+announce turns on both runtimes, and allows fallback-only and announce-only turns.
- `input-provenance.test.ts`: predicate coverage including the resume exclusion.
- `model-fallback.probe.test.ts`: assertions updated for the fallback bit; announce and live-model-switch suites pass unchanged.
- `subagent-announce.format.e2e.test.ts`: the two assertions that still expected the pre-narrowing wording are updated to the narrowed text (`32f17e60`).
- `pnpm tsgo` and `pnpm tsgo:test` are clean locally.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed:** A fallback model serving a turn triggered by an internal completion announcement could convert the announced report into new spawned work (duplicate commits / re-executed tasks), as documented in #92271.

**Real environment tested:** Real OpenClaw runtime source from this branch executed on Linux (WSL2 Ubuntu, Node 22) via tsx against a freshly initialized isolated `OPENCLAW_HOME`. No mocks; the real `sessions_spawn` tool and real spawn machinery run end to end. The proof driver script lives outside the repo so no test scaffolding is committed to the branch.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```bash
cd <branch-checkout> && pnpm exec tsx /home/<user>/openclaw-pr92011-proof.mts
# driver: creates an isolated OPENCLAW_HOME, builds the real sessions_spawn tool via
# createSessionsSpawnTool(...) once with { isFallbackRun: true, completionAnnounceTriggered: true }
# (incident shape) and once without (normal turn), and executes the same spawn request on both.
```

**Evidence after fix:** Copied live console output from the run above.

Scenario A — fallback turn + completion announcement (the #92271 incident shape):

```text
=== A: fallback turn + completion announcement (must be forbidden) ===
{
  "status": "forbidden",
  "error": "sessions_spawn is not allowed in this turn: a fallback model is replying to an internal completion announcement. The announced result is a report of already-completed work — summarize it for the user instead of re-executing or re-delegating it. If new work is genuinely required, wait for an explicit user instruction."
}
```

Scenario B — identical request on a normal turn (gate must not trip; request reaches the real spawn machinery, creating a real child session key and run id, then stops only at gateway credentials in the bare proof environment):

```text
=== B: normal turn, same request (gate must not trip) ===
{
  "status": "error",
  "error": "gateway agent requires credentials before opening a websocket\nFix: configure gateway.auth token/password, pair this device, or pass --token/--password.\nConfig: /tmp/openclaw-proof-PjbSSB/.openclaw/openclaw.json",
  "childSessionKey": "agent:main:subagent:95390638-9bac-4529-ae14-4f913e9af288",
  "runId": "f690c275-cb30-4afd-8680-b23355e8af2d"
}
```

**Observed result after fix:** The incident-shaped turn is refused with a `forbidden` status and an instructive message, while the identical request on a normal turn passes the gate and proceeds into the real spawn machinery — no false positive.

**Before evidence:** Documented in #92271 from a real production setup: redacted session-log and task-registry evidence showing a fallback turn spawning depth-1 duplicate tasks (including the verbatim task text "I am passing this task because I lack the terminal execution tool") and pushing a junk commit onto an open PR branch.

**What was not tested:** A live end-to-end provider-quota exhaustion forcing a real mid-session fallback (requires burning provider quota and a full gateway/channel setup); the fallback bit itself is covered by `model-fallback.probe.test.ts`. Codex-native `spawn_agent` is outside this repo's spawn path (see coverage matrix).

## Scope

This PR **mechanically** enforces the invariant on the **embedded runtime** spawn path (`sessions_spawn`, both `subagent` and `acp` runtimes), plus the content-level evidence guard that travels in announcement text to all harnesses. Two spawn surfaces are intentionally **out of scope** here and tracked as follow-ups:

- **CLI / gateway loopback `sessions_spawn`** — needs the fallback/announce guard inputs threaded through the gateway tool-resolution path (a separate seam; see coverage matrix).
- **Native Codex `spawn_agent`** — owned by `codex-rs`, needs an upstream follow-up.
- **`sessions_send` / `cron` scheduling** — other work-delegating tools remain usable on fallback+announce turns; the "re-delegate" half of the invariant needs the same turn-context gate (or a generalized work-spawning tool policy) on those surfaces. Follow-up.

Because those surfaces remain mechanically unguarded, this PR does **not** claim to fully close the linked issue on its own — using a non-closing reference so the issue stays open until the remaining surfaces are covered.

Refs #92271

target.title: fix(shared): block prototype-polluting keys in JSON schema default hydration
target.body:
## Summary
A plugin whose manifest `configSchema` declares a `__proto__` property can pollute `Object.prototype` process-wide the moment its config is validated. Plugin config validation hydrates JSON Schema defaults automatically for every discovered plugin, so no operator action beyond loading the plugin is required. After the malicious plugin loads, every plain object in the process carries the attacker-supplied property.

## Root cause
`src/shared/json-schema-defaults.ts`, `applyObjectPropertyDefaults`. The property-defaults loop iterates schema-controlled keys and dereferences the matching value slot with no blocked-key guard, unlike the codebase's centralized `isBlockedObjectKey` used at other untrusted object-write boundaries.

Plugin manifests arrive as parsed JSON, so a `__proto__` entry in `properties` is an own key that `Object.entries` yields. For a config value with no own `__proto__`, `value["__proto__"]` reads the inherited `Object.prototype`, and the nested default hydration then writes defaults straight onto it.

before:
```ts
for (const [key, propertySchema] of Object.entries(properties)) {
  const currentValue = value[key];
  const defaultedValue = applySchemaDefaults(
    propertySchema as JsonSchemaValue,
    currentValue,
    ...
  );
  if (defaultedValue !== currentValue || currentValue === undefined) {
    if (defaultedValue !== undefined) {
      value[key] = defaultedValue;
    }
  }
}
```

## Fix
Skip blocked keys (`__proto__`, `prototype`, `constructor`) at each write site in `applyObjectPropertyDefaults`, reusing the existing `isBlockedObjectKey` helper from `src/infra/prototype-keys.ts`.

after:
```ts
for (const [key, propertySchema] of Object.entries(properties)) {
  if (isBlockedObjectKey(key)) {
    continue;
  }
  const currentValue = value[key];
  ...
}
```

## Why this is the right boundary
`applyObjectPropertyDefaults` is the single function that writes default values into a caller-supplied object using schema-derived and value-derived keys, and it routes every plugin/SDK default-hydration call (`applyJsonSchemaDefaults` -> `applySchemaDefaults`). Guarding its three write loops here fixes the vector for every caller rather than at one call site. The `properties` loop is the live global-pollution path (the added regression test fails on pristine `main`); the `patternProperties` and `additionalProperties` loops key off own value keys so they do not globally pollute today, but guarding all three keeps the whole function consistent with `isBlockedObjectKey` usage elsewhere and prevents the vector from reappearing under refactoring. Legitimate config keys named `__proto__`/`constructor`/`prototype` are unrepresentable through a prototype chain anyway, so skipping their default hydration changes no valid behavior.

## Verification
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/shared/json-schema-defaults.test.ts src/plugins/config-schema.test.ts src/infra/prototype-keys.test.ts` passes (17 tests).
- New `applyJsonSchemaDefaults prototype safety` case fails on pristine `main` (`expected 'yes' to be undefined`) and passes with the patch.
- `./node_modules/.bin/oxlint src/shared/json-schema-defaults.ts src/shared/json-schema-defaults.test.ts` clean; `./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check` clean.
- `tsgo` on the changed files reports no new diagnostics (unrelated pre-existing module-resolution errors from broken workspace symlinks in the local checkout are not touched by this diff).

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: a plugin manifest `configSchema` with a `__proto__` property pollutes `Object.prototype` for the whole process during ordinary plugin config validation.
Real environment tested: drove the real plugin config validation builder `buildJsonPluginConfigSchema(...).safeParse({})` from `src/plugins/config-schema.ts` (the same call the plugin loader makes on a discovered plugin), on pristine `origin/main` abfdfd65 and on the patched tree with an identical manifest configSchema; the real default-hydration path, the real TypeBox validation, and the real `Object.prototype` stayed live, nothing mocked.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: `./node_modules/.bin/tsx` on a driver that builds the plugin config schema from the manifest JSON and calls `safeParse({})`, then reads a freshly created object.
Evidence after fix:
```
# BEFORE (pristine origin/main abfdfd65)
safeParse.success: true
Object.prototype.polluted: pwned
freshObject.polluted: pwned
verdict: PROTOTYPE POLLUTED process-wide
# AFTER (this patch, identical inputs)
safeParse.success: true
Object.prototype.polluted: undefined
freshObject.polluted: undefined
verdict: prototype clean
```
Observed result after fix: validating the same plugin manifest leaves `Object.prototype` and newly created objects free of the attacker property, while config validation still succeeds.
What was not tested: no live end-to-end plugin discovery from disk was exercised (the real config-schema builder was driven directly with the manifest JSON); full repo build was not run.

target.title: fix(heartbeat): use fresh Date.now() for schedule advance after runOnce (#104951)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

After ~24h uptime, heartbeat scheduler fires rapid-fire cycles (1-min intervals instead of configured cadence like 30m). The pattern is: 3 healthy cycles → rapid burst → self-recovery or stuck.

The `run()` function captures `const now = startedAt` once at the beginning, then uses that same stale `now` for `advanceAgentSchedule()` AFTER `runOnce()` completes. When `runOnce()` takes significant wall-clock time (network delays, GC pressure after 24h uptime), `computeNextHeartbeatPhaseDueMs({ nowMs: staleNow })` returns a phase-aligned `nextDueMs` that's already past → `Math.max(0, nextDue - Date.now()) = 0` → immediate refire → feedback loop.

## Fix

Use `Date.now()` at each post-`runOnce()` `advanceAgentSchedule()` call site so the next schedule is computed from actual completion time. This is consistent with how `Date.now()` is already used in `scheduleNext()` itself.

### Changes

- **`src/infra/heartbeat-runner.ts`**: 4 call sites changed (`now` → `Date.now()`)
  - Targeted path success (line 1500)
  - Targeted path error catch (line 1508)
  - Fan-out path error catch (line 1530)
  - Fan-out path success (line 1542)
- **`src/infra/heartbeat-runner.scheduler.test.ts`**: New test "recomputes next due from current time after slow runOnce to prevent cadence decay"

### What is NOT changed

- `recordRunBookkeeping(agent, now)` — correctly records run START time for cooldown
- `advanceStaleScheduleAfterDeferral(agent, now, ...)` — no runOnce has run yet at that point
- The pre-runOnce due check `now < agent.nextDueMs` — correct to check at run start time

## Evidence

New test validates the fix:
```typescript
it("recomputes next due from current time after slow runOnce to prevent cadence decay (#104951)", async () => {
  // Simulates runOnce taking 20s wall-clock time via vi.setSystemTime()
  // Verifies: after slow run, next heartbeat does NOT fire within 5s (no 0ms rearm)
  // Verifies: next heartbeat DOES fire after a full interval
});
```

The test uses `vi.setSystemTime(Date.now() + slowRunDurationMs)` inside the mock `runOnce` to simulate wall-clock time passing, then asserts no premature refire (which would happen with the stale `now` bug).

Diff is minimal (4 one-word changes + 1 test):
```
 src/infra/heartbeat-runner.scheduler.test.ts | 34 ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
 src/infra/heartbeat-runner.ts                |  8 +++----
 2 files changed, 38 insertions(+), 4 deletions(-)
```

Closes #104951

target.title: Add plan-first Claw status and remove
target.body:
## Summary

- add experimental `claws status [claw-or-agent]` for agent, workspace-file, partial-state, and package-reference visibility
- add plan-first `claws remove <claw-or-agent> --dry-run --json` with separate `--yes` consent
- reuse canonical agent deletion and identity-safe managed-file cleanup
- uninstall a final, unchanged Claw-installed plugin or skill through its existing owner lifecycle
- retain pre-existing, shared, pending, modified, missing, or ambiguous artifacts and report why

## Scope

This is the status/remove slice for the grouped one-Claw/one-agent contract. Package names resolve an install only when unambiguous; final agent ids always work and disambiguate repeated adds.

Remove revalidates the agent digest, managed files, and package decisions before mutation. Agent drift and unsafe workspace paths block the plan. Missing files are already removed, locally modified files are retained, and unchanged files are moved to nonce staging paths before final digest validation and deletion.

Package removal is ownership-aware. A completed `claw-installed` skill is removed only from its owning agent workspace after strict ClawHub origin, lock, version, and `SKILL.md` digest validation. A plugin is removed only when no other Claw references its ClawHub package and its installed identity/version still match; execution delegates to the canonical plugin uninstall command. When the original installing Claw is removed while another Claw still references a global plugin, ownership transfers to a surviving reference so the eventual final removal remains correct. Package-plan changes after dry-run fail revalidation instead of escalating consent.

If package or file cleanup fails after the agent config commit, the root ledger remains partial and subordinate references stay available for status/doctor recovery. All commands remain gated by `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`, and JSON contracts remain experimental.

## Stack

- RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27
- Depends on: #102228 package installation, ownership, and references

- Next: #102306 portable export from the same provenance ledger

target.title: fix(gateway): don't retire parent Codex binding when creating a detached dashboard child
target.body:
Fixes #106778

## What Problem This Solves

Creating a dashboard child from an active Codex-backed channel session (Control UI → new dashboard chat — an ordinary child creation, not a fork) succeeds but **retires the parent session's Codex binding**, even though the parent remains the channel's current session. The next inbound parent turn then fails permanently with `Codex binding generation was retired`, recoverable only by manual SQLite surgery.

Root-cause chain (all on current `main`):
1. `createGatewaySession` emits a terminal `session_end(reason:"new")` on the **parent** for any parent-linked child when `emitCommandHooks === true` — `src/gateway/session-create-service.ts`.
2. The Codex extension treats `"new"` as terminal (`ENDED_SESSION_REASONS`) and its `session_end` handler calls `bindingStore.retireSessionGeneration()` — `extensions/codex/index.ts:48,274`.
3. The next lease attempt observes the retired generation and throws `Codex binding generation was retired`.

A detached dashboard child (its own `agent:<id>:dashboard:*` key) runs **in parallel** — it does not replace the parent as the channel's current session, so emitting a terminal `session_end` on the parent is wrong.

## Approach

The parent rolls over — terminal `session_end` on the parent, `session_start` on the child — only when the child **succeeds** it. That disposition cannot be inferred from the child's key shape: the server keeps no current-session pointer, so a key namespace cannot prove succession (the earlier `startsWith("dashboard:")` gate was a heuristic). The caller declares it explicitly via a new optional `succeedsParent` flag on `sessions.create`; the gate reads the flag:

```ts
const childSucceedsParent = params.fork !== true && params.succeedsParent === true;
```

The namespace invariant is enforced by a **loud boundary validation** rather than silent inference: `succeedsParent` requires an explicit non-dashboard successor key and conflicts with `fork`; a keyless/minted or dashboard-namespaced child (auto-managed, detached) is rejected with `INVALID_REQUEST`. A mis-declared succession therefore fails loudly instead of silently retiring a still-active parent's binding.

- **Only TUI `/new`** (an explicit `tui-*` successor) declares `succeedsParent: true` — it still emits the parent `session_end` + child `session_start`.
- **Every other create path** — minted dashboard child (webchat "new chat"), fork, catalog/work child — is parallel by default and unchanged: no parent `session_end`, child `session_start` fires.
- **Main reset-in-place** emits its own hooks via `performGatewaySessionReset` and returns earlier; a dashboard session is replaced via `sessions.reset` (which retires its binding in place), never a create-succession.
- The parent's `before_reset` / `command:new` hooks (documented Control UI behavior, #76957) are untouched.

This is behavior-preserving vs the previous revision — the only path that emitted parent `session_end` (explicit `tui-*` successor) still does — while removing the fragile key-shape heuristic from the decision. Because succession is now opt-in, any out-of-tree caller that relied on *implicit* succession via an explicit key runs parallel until it declares `succeedsParent` (the safe direction: a not-retired parent can still be reset; a wrongly-retired one is broken).

**Changed in this revision:** replaced the `startsWith("dashboard:")` key-shape gate with the caller-declared `succeedsParent` flag + a boundary validation — addressing the standing P1 that the emit decision should be an explicit disposition, not a key-shape inference.

**Maintainer note.** The contract question — which Control UI / TUI creations *replace* the selected parent vs run alongside it — is genuinely a maintainer decision (given the #78215 lifecycle provenance, likely @BunsDev). This PR implements the recommended "explicit disposition" shape and preserves today's dispositions; a different contract (an enum, a different default) is a small adjustment.

Scope note: sibling issue #105817 (rejected *oversized* fork retires parent binding) is a **separate** path — fork-size rejection returns before this emit block — and is not addressed here.

## Evidence

### Persisted-state consequence — proven in-boundary over a real store

The destructive step lives in the Codex extension, and its bundled suite already asserts it over a **real** `createCodexAppServerBindingStore`: `session_end(reason:"new")` retires the generation (`read() → undefined` — the `{"state":"cleared","retired":true}` tombstone #106778 reports), while non-terminal reasons (`shutdown`, `restart`, `compaction`) leave it intact. So the persisted mutation is real and reason-selective — suppressing the parent `session_end` for a parallel child is exactly what keeps the binding alive.

### Gate A/B + validation (real gateway session-create path, deterministic)

`server.sessions.reset-hooks.test.ts` toggles only the disposition:

```
explicit tui-* successor (succeedsParent)        → parent session_end(reason:"new") + child session_start
minted dashboard child (default)                 → no parent session_end; child session_start
fork                                             → no parent session_end
succeedsParent + {dashboard-keyed|keyless|fork}  → INVALID_REQUEST (no hooks)
```

target.title: fix: external plugin tabs fail under gateway auth
target.body:
Closes #107255

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users opening an external plugin Control UI tab would see the embedded panel fail with `401 Unauthorized` when the plugin route uses Gateway auth and the Gateway is running in token/password auth mode.

## Why This Change Was Made

External plugin tab descriptors already advertise gateway-local `path` values, and the Control UI should keep rendering those tabs as ordinary sandboxed iframes. This change issues short-lived, signed, HttpOnly plugin-tab cookies after authenticated Control UI read auth, then accepts those cookies only inside the plugin HTTP route auth stage.

The cookie handoff is now bounded in two ways:

- Browser cookie `Path` is scoped to each advertised external plugin tab path.
- The signed payload carries the same route path and the current shared Gateway auth generation, so sibling plugin routes and stale credentials are rejected before runtime scopes are derived.

Direct unauthenticated plugin route requests still return `401`, Gateway credentials are not placed in iframe URLs, and external tab rendering stays a normal `iframe src` load.

## User Impact

Operators can open external plugin Control UI tabs whose HTTP routes are protected with `auth: "gateway"` instead of making those routes public, switching to plugin-managed auth, or putting Gateway credentials in iframe URLs.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/control-ui.http.test.ts src/gateway/server.plugin-http-auth.test.ts`

target.body:
<!-- submission-timestamps:start -->
First submitted: July 6, 2026, 10:00 PM (US Eastern Time) / 02:00 UTC.
Last body edit: July 15, 2026, 3:56 AM (US Eastern Time) / 07:56 UTC.
Latest head commit: July 15, 2026, 3:47 AM (US Eastern Time) / 07:47 UTC.
<!-- submission-timestamps:end -->

Closes #101204

## What Problem This Solves

A configured but temporarily missing built-in TTS API-key SecretRef currently aborts Gateway startup and takes unrelated chat, auth, tools, channels, and plugins offline even though only speech synthesis needs that credential. This PR keeps the first activating startup available while preserving strict failure for every non-activating, reload, restart-check, config-write, malformed-ref, policy, provider, contract, mismatch, and invalid-value path.

## Summary

A missing built-in TTS provider API-key SecretRef no longer aborts an otherwise healthy Gateway during the first activating startup. The affected TTS provider remains unconfigured, startup emits a structured warning, and unrelated chat, auth, tools, channels, and plugins continue to start.

The exception is deliberately narrow. It requires all of the following:

- the lifecycle reason is `startup`;
- the operation will activate the prepared snapshot (`activate === true`);
- no active secrets runtime snapshot exists;
- the assignment is a built-in TTS provider API key explicitly marked optional; and
- resolution failed with the matching missing-value error for that exact ref.

Non-activating startup preparation, restart checks, reloads, config-write preflight, malformed refs, policy/security failures, provider failures, contract failures, mismatched errors, and invalid resolved value shapes remain fail-closed.

## Breaking changes

There is no config-shape, RPC, persistence, package, or dependency change. Failure timing changes for one credential class: a missing built-in TTS API-key SecretRef is reported as a startup warning and fails locally when that TTS provider is used, rather than aborting the entire first activating Gateway startup.

## Why / user impact

Built-in TTS is an optional capability, but SecretRef activation previously treated its API keys as credentials required by the whole Gateway. Operators may now keep an optional ElevenLabs or other built-in TTS SecretRef configured while its value is temporarily absent. The provider remains unavailable until the ref resolves, while unrelated Gateway capabilities stay online.

The stricter sibling paths are unchanged: reload, restart-check, non-activating startup preparation, and config-write preflight reject the unresolved ref and preserve the last-known-good runtime/config.

## Implementation

- `src/gateway/server-startup-config.ts` owns the lifecycle gate. Optional missing-value degradation is enabled only for `reason === "startup"`, `activate === true`, and an absent active runtime snapshot.
- The lifecycle gate is layered onto the current mainline `resolveGatewayStartupSecretProjection` contract. `sourceConfig` remains the recoverable full source, while an `assignmentConfig` may suppress unsafe channel assignments during crash-loop recovery; this PR does not collapse those responsibilities back into one pruned config.
- `src/secrets/runtime-config-collectors-tts.ts` marks only built-in TTS provider API-key assignments as optional at startup.
- `src/secrets/resolve-errors.ts` owns typed provider/ref errors and the exact missing-value classifier; `src/secrets/resolve.ts` assigns those codes at env/file/exec and provider-contract boundaries.
- `src/secrets/runtime-optional-assignments.ts` owns required/optional partitioning, independent optional resolution, warning emission, and redaction registration.

target.title: refactor(gateway-client): expose request dispatch boundary
target.body:
Related: #96230

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-internal callers can observe a request result or a later `accepted` response, but cannot distinguish a failure before the request frame entered the local WebSocket transport from a failure after dispatch. That distinction is required before later restart-recovery work can make conservative retry or refund decisions without guessing from promise settlement.

This is the first independently reviewable dependency extracted from #96230. The original PR remains frozen while its behavior is split into ordered, narrower changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The protocol client is the only layer that owns the synchronous `socket.send(...)` boundary, so this adds an optional `onDispatched` observer immediately after `send` returns successfully and routes it through the existing callback-isolation helper. The package client and high-level `callGateway` wrapper forward the same observer without changing request frames, protocol versions, timeout/abort cleanup, reconnect behavior, or `onAccepted` response semantics.

The observer contract is intentionally narrow: it means the request frame was handed to the local WebSocket transport. It does not mean the Gateway/server accepted or processed the request. The request option type lives in a dedicated small module and is re-exported from the existing protocol-client module, preserving import and structural type compatibility. `GatewayClient` forwards that shared option shape as a unit, then overrides only its normalized `expectFinal` and `timeoutMs` values; this keeps the oversized implementation LOC-neutral without deleting unrelated comments.

This is a root-cause boundary fix: higher layers no longer need to infer whether transport dispatch happened. The gateway-client package is private and the new field is additive and optional. The bundled LanceDB memory plugin checked whether the `memories` table existed and then created it in a separate operation. Two OpenClaw processes initializing the same database could both observe the table as absent, race during creation, and fail startup with a duplicate-create error.

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.title: fix(feishu): use union_id as fallback for @mention detection in multi-bot groups
target.body:
## Problem

Fixes #40768

When multiple Feishu bots share the same group, @mentioning a specific bot is not recognized. The bot logs `message in group ... did not mention bot` even though it's correctly mentioned.

## Root Cause

Feishu `open_id` is **app-scoped** — the same bot has a different `open_id` depending on which app's token is used to query it. Confirmed by querying the same message with two different bot tokens:

```
# Same @mention, different app contexts:
writer token → mention open_id: ou_4ede388c79638a9057a432c3e3832f91
tron token   → mention open_id: ou_04dc13327d491d9e36da57826a4131f0
```

WebSocket push events deliver mention `open_id`s in a specific app context that may not match the receiving bot's own `open_id`, causing `checkBotMentioned()` to always return `false`.

## Fix

`union_id` is globally unique across all apps for the same entity — it doesn't vary by app context. This PR:

1. Fetches `union_id` alongside `open_id` from `bot/v3/info` at startup
2. Stores it in a new `botUnionIds` map in monitor state
3. Passes it through to `checkBotMentioned()` as a fallback
4. Matches mentions by `union_id` when `open_id` doesn't match

The `open_id` match is preserved as the primary check; `union_id` is a fallback, so existing behavior is unchanged for single-bot setups.

## Files Changed

- `types.ts`: add `botUnionId` to `FeishuProbeResult`
- `probe.ts`: extract `union_id` from `bot/v3/info` response
- `monitor.startup.ts`: propagate `botUnionId` through `FeishuMonitorBotIdentity`
- `monitor.state.ts`: add `botUnionIds` map with proper clear/delete
- `monitor.account.ts`: store/clear `botUnionId`, pass to `handleFeishuMessage`
- `bot.ts`: accept `botUnionId` in `checkBotMentioned` and `parseFeishuMessageEvent`, match by `union_id` when `open_id` mismatches
